title: Pilot evaluation of detached youth work
official: Pilot area-level randomised controlled trial of detached youth work
summary:
Background and study aims
Detached youth work is a form of youth work that takes place in public spaces where young people choose to spend their time, such as parks, streets and town centres. Detached youth workers go to where young people are, rather than expecting them to come to a youth centre. Detached youth workers build trusting relationships with young people and offer support and provide informal learning. Young people take part voluntarily and can come and go as they want.
Despite a long history in England, there is very little strong evidence about whether detached youth work reduces youth crime and antisocial behaviour. This study aims to test whether a large-scale trial of the impact of detached youth work could work in future. It does this by running a smaller pilot trial first. The pilot has four aims: to test whether this kind of trial is feasible; to look for early signs of whether detached youth work affects local crime and antisocial behaviour; to understand how the work is delivered and experienced; and to estimate what it costs to deliver.

Who can participate?
The study focuses on small, defined public areas called 'patches' where young people are known to gather, rather than on individually recruited people. Forty patches have been identified across four regions of England.
In the patches that receive detached youth work, any young people aged 10 to 17 years can choose to engage with the detached youth workers. Engagement is always voluntary. Young people aged 16 years and over may also be invited to take part in surveys or creative research activities, with their informed consent. Youth workers, managers, residents and other local stakeholders may take part in interviews and focus groups as part of the study.

What does the study involve?
The 40 patches are randomly put into two groups: 20 receive detached youth work and 20 carry on with 'services as usual'. Allocating patches at random helps us understand whether any changes in crime and antisocial behaviour are because of the detached youth work.
In the delivery patches, trained youth workers spend at least four hours each week in public spaces. They build relationships with young people, offer informal support and activities, and respond to young people’s priorities. Before delivery begins, there is a 6-month period in which youth workers get to know the area and the community.
The study measures impact mainly by looking at police-recorded crime and antisocial behaviour in each patch. Researchers also carry out interviews and creative activities with young people, youth workers, managers and community members to understand how the work is delivered and what difference it makes. A separate cost analysis looks at how much it costs to deliver the service. The team will also analyse historical police data from other areas to estimate the likely size of any effect, which is needed to plan the needed sample size of a future impact study.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Young people in the delivery patches will have access to detached youth work, including relationship building, informal education and signposting to other services. The wider benefit is better evidence about whether and how detached youth work helps young people and communities.
Young people in the control patches will not receive detached youth work during the study but will continue to receive any other services available in their area. Control areas have committed to not delivering detached youth work for the study period, but they can deliver other forms of youth work to address arising risks/needs of young people. 
While researchers will not ask sensitive questions, there is a small risk that people taking part in research activities may bring up sensitive topics voluntarily, and they might find some questions uncomfortable. Taking part is voluntary, and they can stop at any time. All detached youth workers and researchers are trained in safeguarding, and the team has robust data protection and ethical procedures in place. The police data used is anonymised and cannot be linked to individuals.

Where is the study run from?
The study is run by the Centre for Evidence and Implementation (CEI), working with Bryson Purdon Social Research, Dr David McLennan (DJM Social Research) and Professor Alex Sutherland (University of Oxford). Detached youth work is delivered across four regional consortia in England: Greater Manchester; Wiltshire and Swindon; Leeds, Wakefield and Barnsley; and Middlesbrough and Stockton (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study began its co-design phase in October 2025. Set-up runs from April to September 2026; randomisation will take place in July 2026 after study registration. A six-month reconnaissance period begins in October 2026, followed by 12 months of detached youth work delivery from April 2027 to March 2028. Final analysis and reporting take place from mid-2028, with findings expected to be shared by March 2029. In total the study runs for about three and a half years.

Who is funding the study?
Youth Endowment Fund (YEF) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Amy Hall, amy.hall@ceiglobal.org

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Randomisation at the 'patch' level, i.e., pre-defined geographic areas of between 10 and 100 hectares. Patches will be selected prior to randomisation and will not change for the duration of the study. Four consortia will each identify 10 patches, providing a total of 40 patches. Any young people (aged 10-18 years) who engage with the detached youth workers will be considered eligible within the patches. Patches must meet these eligibility criteria: 
1. No detached youth work has been delivered within the patch from October 2025 to the start of the reconnaissance period (October 2026).
2. There is evidence of an issue of youth crime/ASB that detached youth work might help to reduce. This criterion does not have a numeric threshold, acknowledging variation across contexts and communities. However, consortia were provided with historical data about national averages to help justify what might be considered ‘high’ or ‘normal’ rates of incidents per hectare. 
3. The patch is an appropriate size for DYW teams to cover it within one session while also being large enough to allow for some movement of young people, for example, between indoor and outdoor spaces that are favoured differently by young people depending on seasonal changes. Consortia have been asked to identify patches of between 10 and 100 hectares in size. If larger patches are proposed, then consortia are expected to provide evidence that these patches can be covered effectively by the detached youth work team each week. 
4. The patch covers an area where a reachable population of young people are known or observed to gather frequently. Consortia are expected to consider young people’s movement between meeting places, and patches should therefore be designed to accommodate some movement.
5. The consortia have sufficient local knowledge, relationships and commitment of relevant organisations to deliver, monitor and influence what takes place in the patch throughout the duration of the project.
Exclusion criteria:
Patches that do not meet the eligibility criteria
